text:
The passage rewards attention to what is missing. Sarah is nowhere in Genesis 22, and the book announces her death in the verse immediately following the chapter. The scene implies, though it never says, that something in the household did not survive the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants; Isaac is not mentioned. At the point where a lesser story would linger, the telling turns away. Its silence is testimony.

It may be answered that this is only the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains. This may perhaps, in some sense, be true; yet the narrator elsewhere reports what characters feel. Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence here is deliberate. The narrative knows what it is doing. Restraint, in this voice, becomes a kind of accusation.
